figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Why modeling is hard to evaluate, and what TB-MathModel changes. (a) In the status quo an LLM judge grades a report on organisation while the numbers are never checked. (b) TB-MathModel runs the problem, attachments, and figures in a terminal container, requires one structured artifact, scores it one-sidedly against an O-award reproduction, and verifies feasibility with a gate and Lean certificates—so a plausible-but-infeasible answer is caught.
figures.headline: Status-quo judging leaves numbers unchecked, whereas the terminal pipeline catches plausible answers that violate feasibility.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The TB-MathModel construction and evaluation pipeline. Build: official statements, attachments, and PDF figures are compiled into a task directory. Run: the agent works inside a network-isolated terminal container and writes one JSON artifact. Evaluate: the artifact is scored by a direction-aware, one-sided panel against an O-award reproduction, and independently checked by a programmatic feasibility gate plus a Lean 4 certificate layer; a failed gate zeroes the task.
figures.headline: The pipeline runs agents in isolated containers and zeroes any task whose artifact fails the feasibility gate.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Left: multi-reference O-Eval versus cost (log scale)—the Pareto frontier is compressed, with near-frontier scores at two orders of magnitude lower cost. Centre: O-Eval per entry. Right: O-Eval by suite, showing the CUMCM–MCM gap.
figures.headline: Near-frontier scores come at about two orders of magnitude lower cost, and open-ended suites score lower than engineering suites.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: An official statement figure, cropped from the CUMCM 2023 A PDF and delivered inline in the prompt. 21 such figures across 6 tasks are load-bearing: the final answer depends on reading them.
figures.headline: An official statement figure is delivered inline, since 21 such figures across 6 tasks are needed to reach the final answer.

abstract: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023–2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification—a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean 4 obligations—with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58%, while the \$2.54 open model holds 59.81% at $1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/terminal-bench-math-modeling.

sections.body: Contest modeling asks for assumptions, a model, a solution and a recommendation, not a single number. Existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, which leaves the reported numbers unchecked. Table 1 places TB-MathModel against three such benchmarks. Only TB-MathModel combines a complete contest problem, an agentic terminal run, an executable verifier, physical-feasibility checking and a machine-checkable proof on a multimodal task. The benchmark covers 18 tasks and 21 figures. The section names three design problems: there is no single ground truth, anchoring on one paper creates asymmetric failure, and plausible but infeasible answers escape anchor comparison.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing benchmarks miss modeling; TB-MathModel is the first to make full contest problems agentic, verifiable and terminal.

sections.body: The section groups related work into agent benchmarks, mathematical and operations-research benchmarks, modeling benchmarks and verification. Software and terminal benchmarks measure repository edits and command-line tasks but attach no feasibility contract. Operations-research systems certify feasibility of a given formulation, yet they cannot certify the abstraction and do not require assumptions or a recommendation. The closest modeling work is Mamo, which is solver-grounded and narrow, and ModelingBench, which relies on an LLM judge and is not reproducible. The authors use the Lean 4 prover to audit the benchmark's own feasibility decisions, which they say is new to their knowledge.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier modeling benchmarks score a single solver artifact or an LLM-judged report, and none is agentic, verifiable and terminal.

sections.body: Each of the 18 contest tasks is built into an instruction file, an agent container with attachments and an output schema, a verifier container, and an oracle that reproduces an Outstanding-award paper. The agent must return one JSON artifact. Each task has 2–6 scored metrics, 60 in total, each with a direction: higher or lower is better, target value, or exact value. Directional metrics never score below 1.0 at or beyond the anchor. Task scores average over every outstanding paper for the problem, 99 in total, of which 94 yield the scored quantity. A programmatic gate covers 18/18 tasks through six decidable forms, and a Lean 4 layer adds 624 obligations. A failed gate sets the task score to zero.
sections.heading: The TB-MathModel Benchmark
sections.headline: Scoring against a panel of outstanding papers, with one-sided rewards and a feasibility gate, defines the benchmark.

sections.body: Seven multimodal model and harness entries each ran three seeds on all 18 tasks, using the same scorer and anchors. GPT-6 Astra + codex scored 64.58±2.93 and Fable 5.1 + claude-code scored 63.11±1.33 on O-Eval. DeepSeek-Flash + opencode scored 59.81±1.25 at a cost of 2.54 USD per pass. Changing only the harness moved O-Eval by at most 0.07 pp, so the authors conclude the board measures the model. The authors state that per-seed deviations reach 2.93 pp, so adjacent rows are not significantly separated. Running DeepSeek-Flash at its maximum reasoning tier lowered its score to 48.11%. The hard gate invalidated 7 cells, mostly heliostat answers.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: The newest flagships top seven multimodal entries, while a 2.54 USD open model reaches 59.81 at about 1/100 the cost.

sections.body: The paper presents TB-MathModel as the first agentic and verifiable terminal benchmark of 18 real modeling problems. Scored against human outstanding papers, the newest flagships lead, with GPT-6 Astra at 64.58% and Fable 5.1 at 63.11%. DeepSeek-Flash holds 59.81% at 1/100 the cost. The authors argue that a fast gate covering every task, paired with a proof assistant that audits the gate, is the transferable idea. Because the reward is reproducible, the trajectories can also serve as training material, and the paper proposes directions drawn from its findings.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: TB-MathModel gives a reproducible, machine-checkable signal, and its two-layer feasibility design is the transferable idea.

sections.body: Each task is normalised against one reproducible Outstanding-award solution with recorded provenance. The authors name a multi-paper panel as the natural extension, and the panel size depends on how many outstanding reports exist for each problem, from 1 to 18 papers. On the tennis momentum task, 10 of 11 papers reach the opposite conclusion from the anchor, so the task is marked literature-split and kept out of headline rankings. The verification layers decide unit, range and internal-consistency questions but not external physical truth, which is checked only where an independent replay exists. Scores are three-seed means, and the authors say the task format carries over to engineering and cross-disciplinary problems.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Modeling has no single correct answer, so panel sizes range from 1 to 18 papers and literature-split tasks are excluded from headline rankings.

sections.body: Statements, attachments and figures are official CUMCM and MCM material used for research evaluation. The authors state they do not redistribute outstanding-award solutions, and the reproduction code derives from a public corpus with per-task provenance. Users must confirm the licence terms for their own redistribution. The authors say the benchmark measures and improves the modeling workflow of LLM agents rather than automating work presented as a team's own. They also state that fully automated evaluation keeps the cost of broad participation low.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Official outstanding-paper solutions are not redistributed, and users should confirm licence terms before redistributing the material.

sections.body: Every entry in Table 2 is an LLM agent, which is the object of measurement. Language models also helped draft prose and check the internal consistency of LaTeX and numbers. The authors state that benchmark construction, scoring rules, feasibility checks and Lean obligations were specified, implemented and verified by the authors. All numerical results are produced by the released scripts.
sections.heading: Use of Large Language Models
sections.headline: Language models were both the systems under test and drafting aids, while the authors specified and verified all benchmark components.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the dataset composition, a per-task table, and an explicit statement that there is no train, validation or test split. Appendix B records the software and hardware environment and the network isolation policy. Appendix C lists per-entry configuration and cost accounting. Appendix D disambiguates the three objects called baseline. Appendix E reproduces the prompt template. Appendix F gives the case-study numerics. Appendix G gives the scoring formulas, excluded metrics and hard-gate decisions. Appendix H catalogues the 624 Lean obligations, the trust audit and the discrimination suite.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists dataset composition, environment, per-entry configuration, scoring formulas, and the Lean obligation catalogue.
